source.title: Automated Program Repair in the Era of Large Pre-trained Language Models
source.authors: Chun Xia; Yu-Xiang Wei; Ling-Ming Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It compares downstream program-repair performance across models of different parameter counts. This is a conceptual test of whether downstream performance improves with scale, using repair outcomes rather than held-out language-model loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports APR outcomes by model size, dataset, and repair setting, which bear on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit loss power laws, test loss extrapolation, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It also does not systematically test architecture shape at fixed parameter count or scaling laws in other modalities. Reported timing, compilation rates, entropy, and patch-ranking outcomes do not test the named versions and are not included as rows. The single-line-generation results in Table V are left out under the row limit; the complete-function and infilling results provide the model-size comparisons recorded here.
record.test_reason: It compares program-repair bug-fix counts across sizes within model families (GPT-Neo/J/NeoX, all trained on The Pile; INCODER 1.3B/6.7B). This bears on V6 (downstream performance improving with scale) in a new task setting. It fits no curve and measures no pretraining loss, so it is not T1 or T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also say performance 'consistently increases' within the GPT family on all datasets. The QuixBugs-Java numbers in Table III (4→3→3) and some Table V cells do not fully bear this out. They also report a steep speed cost: GPT-NeoX is 71x slower than GPT-Neo 125M.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares APR bug-fix counts across pretrained models and parameter sizes; it does not measure language-model loss or fit scaling-law curves.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported APR performance varies by dataset and repair setting; the authors also note differences between models trained on The Pile and code-focused Codex.
record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty estimates for the repair counts. Correctness of plausible patches was determined by manual inspection. The authors discuss possible training-data leakage and note that findings may not generalize beyond the tested datasets and languages. Model comparisons also vary in architecture, training data, and code specialization, so parameter count is not isolated.
record.rows_left_out: Table V reports single-line-generation outcomes for additional model and dataset combinations. These are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit after recording the complete-function results from Table III and correct-code-infilling results from Table IV. The paper's speed, compilation-rate, entropy, and patch-ranking results were also excluded because they do not measure the downstream-performance scaling relation in V6.

untested.parts: Predictability in the quantitative sense: no fitted trend, no extrapolation, no link to pretraining loss. The study compares only a handful of sizes per family, with no uncertainty estimates.

record.verdict_notes: Kept as tests/T3 for V6 only; V1-V5 and V7 are untouched. The Codex and CodeT5 rows are cross-family comparisons and stay cannot_determine as single points. The smallest model in each family serves as the baseline. Table V, declared left out, has further non-monotonic cells: QuixBugs-Java GPT-Neo 1.3B 19 vs 2.7B 16; Defects4J 2.0 GPT-Neo 2.7B 16 vs GPT-J 12. There is a leakage caveat: 15% of the checked fixes from open models appear in the training data. No uncertainty estimates are reported; correctness was judged manually.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute; power-law form and orders of magnitude.
Fitting on smaller language-model runs and predicting held-out loss on much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study measures APR outcomes, not a broad range of downstream tasks or their relationship to pretraining loss; it does not fit a predictive curve or quantify prediction accuracy.
The study does not vary loss-fitting choices or test whether fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations depend on setup.

relationships.condition: GPT-Neo/J/NeoX family (The Pile), complete function generation, Defects4J 1.2, Defects4J 2.0, ManyBugs
relationships.reason: Correct fixes rise at every size step from 125M to 20B (r1-r5, r7-r11, r25-r29). ManyBugs counts are very small.
relationships.display_finding: Correct fixes increased at every size step from 125M to 20B across all three datasets, although very few ManyBugs fixes were achieved.

relationships.condition: GPT family, complete function generation, QuixBugs-Java and QuixBugs-Python
relationships.reason: The trend holds overall (125M to 20B), but the middle sizes are flat or reversed: Java 4→3→3 (r14-r16), Python 4→4 (r20-r21).
relationships.display_finding: Overall performance improves from 125M to 20B, but intermediate Java results fall from 4 to 3 to 3 and Python results remain at 4.

relationships.condition: INCODER 1.3B vs 6.7B, correct code infilling, all five datasets
relationships.reason: 6.7B fixes more bugs on every dataset, with only small gains on QuixBugs-Python and ManyBugs (r32-r33, r36-r37, r40-r41, r44-r45, r48-r49).
relationships.display_finding: The 6.7B model fixed more bugs on every dataset, with only small gains on QuixBugs-Python and ManyBugs.

relationships.condition: Comparisons across model families with different training data
relationships.reason: Codex 12B beats GPT-NeoX 20B on every dataset (e.g. 63 vs 18 on Defects4J 1.2), so parameter count alone does not predict repair ability across families (r5, r6, r12, r18, r24, r30).
relationships.display_finding: Codex 12B outperforms GPT-NeoX 20B on every dataset, including 63 versus 18 on Defects4J 1.2, showing that size alone cannot predict performance across families.
